tracks.title: Change it while it's running
tracks.text: Lesson 02 point 9 — hot swap. A sub-lesson, under nexus… the engine you own. [curious] Here's the whole idea, up front. Everywhere else, updating a running system means a deploy train — rebuild, restart, reconnect… pray. The Nexus doesn't. Because a name-to-bytes binding is data… not code. An update isn't mutating the running thing. It's adding a new immutable file… and repointing a name. In-flight work finishes on the old bytes. And nothing… reboots.

tracks.title: The deploy train versus living software
tracks.text: First — the deploy train, versus living software. For ordinary software a restart is merely annoying. For living software — agents working continuously, inside an engine you and they both touch — it's lethal twice over. [sighs] Lethal the first way when an agent authors a tool mid-session. It just wrote a command it needs now, three steps into a task. If getting that tool live means a CI run and a restart… the agent's work is gone before the tool arrives. And lethal the second way when a human pushes a fix to a system an agent is actively working in. The old answer was a deploy — rebuild, restart, and drop whatever the agent had in flight. The cowboy answer was worse — tar the new files over SSH, straight onto the box, and clobber the agent's half-written state. One path drops the work… the other overwrites it. The reader has been burned by both.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. A hot swap is a loaded artifact — a toolkit command, a kernel, an agent definition, content — replaced in a running Nexus by repointing a name at new content-addressed bytes. In-flight work finishes on the old bytes… and nothing reboots. The lineage is Erlang's hot code loading — the famous trick of replacing a module in a live VM without dropping calls. The Nexus gets the same effect… one level up. Not on VM modules… but on the artifacts the engine loads. Same spirit, different layer. And content addressing does the job the BEAM magic did below it.

tracks.title: The binding is the whole trick
tracks.text: Now — the binding is the whole trick. And it's smaller than you expect. The live system is just a tiny map… from names to files. When you run a command by name, the engine looks the name up and runs the file it points at. Re-registering a name that already exists doesn't append… or version. It replaces the binding in place. The source even labels it, in capital letters — hot swap. [curious] Let me walk you through the one trace that matters — three players. First, caller A, already running. Second, the registry — the name-to-file map. And third, caller B, who shows up later. Caller A invokes slugify… and the registry resolves the path at call time, handing back the old file, nine-f-two-c. Mid-run, a re-register lands a new sha for the same name. Caller A keeps going — and finishes on the old bytes, because old files are never deleted… a new sha is simply a new file. Then caller B invokes the same name… and gets the new sha, four-b-seven-e. Same name… two immutable files… the map moved between them. [excited] That's the confidence claim, exactly. You can change a live system an agent depends on, without breaking its work — because a call resolves its file when it starts, and keeps that file to the end.

tracks.title: Why the swap is safe
tracks.text: Why is the swap safe? Because the files it points at are immutable… and self-naming. Picture the pipeline as five steps. First — source: bytes from a build, and the same input always yields the same bytes. Second — sha256: hash those bytes, and the hash is the filename. Third — the dot-wasm file: written only if absent, and old files never deleted. Fourth — repoint: the registry binds the name to this path, replacing in place. And fifth, on boot — reload-persisted re-registers from a manifest, no rebuild. The verdict of that picture, in one line — the filename is the proof, so a tampered byte can't masquerade as the trusted one. [curious] And that check runs at run time… not just register time. The registry re-hashes the file when it loads it, and refuses a mismatch. So even if something altered the bytes on disk between registration and use — the classic race — the swap fails closed… rather than running poisoned code. And the swaps survive a reboot without rebuilding anything. A tiny manifest records name… to addressed path. On boot, the engine re-registers every entry from it — no rebuild, no fetch.

tracks.title: Swap by self-authoring
tracks.text: One swap primitive… three ways to drive it. First vehicle — swap by self-authoring. The in-session swap. An agent re-registers a command it just rebuilt… in seconds. The whole cycle — write the source, build it, address it, register it — runs entirely inside the wasm sandbox. Even the compiler is wasm. Six languages build inline — rust, c, zig, javascript, typescript, and go. And the built command is capped by the instance's policy profile… self-authoring can never widen the granted capability set. An agent can write itself a sharper tool. It can't write itself a bigger blast radius. [curious] You can drive it by hand. Run wb toolkit build-inline slugify rust, on a source file. The engine answers — built and registered command slugify, rust, arrow, build-commands-nine-f-two-c-dot-wasm. Run it via the Dock. Now the swap — edit the source, re-run the same command. Different bytes… different sha… say four-b-seven-e. Ask the engine what's bound now, and current-of-slugify shows the new path. The old file is still on disk — a call mid-flight when you swapped finished on it. Two immutable files… one name… the map moved. [chuckles] Try that trick on a built-in like jq, and you get error… reserved name. And the durability ladder is session, to workspace, to registry — promote materializes an inline command as a real toolkit, persisting the source… not just the bytes.

tracks.title: Swap by push
tracks.text: Second vehicle — swap by push. A git push that goes live within one tick. Turn on gitops, and at the top of every keeper tick — before the agent runs — the engine reconciles the tenant repo. The critical word is integrate… not overwrite. It snapshots any dirty agent work first, fetches origin, then does a real git merge. [curious] Let me walk the flow as a story. A human pushes a fix to skills-seo-dot-org. On the next tick — the engine snapshots dirty work as a work-in-progress commit. Then fetches. Then merges. If the merge is clean… it applies, publishes content, deploys the built app… and it's live — the next agent run reads it. But there's a second branch. If the same file changed on both sides… the merge aborts, rolls back, and returns a conflict with the file listed — reported… and left for a human. Never silently overwritten. Two things keep that merge clean in practice. First — the code-data path split. CODE — the app source, the agent def, design-dot-org, skills — is what humans and CI push. DATA — content, blog, the board — is what the agent commits. Disjoint paths… so they almost never touch the same file. Second — when they do collide, the abort is honest, not destructive. And live here is literal… and atomic. The runtime publishes inside the commit path — because the lander once shipped blogs that were committed… but served a 404. So commit and publish became one operation. This page owns the swap semantics… the gitops lesson owns the plumbing underneath.

tracks.title: The zero-mechanism swap
tracks.text: Third vehicle — the zero-mechanism swap. And the point is that it has no mechanism at all. The keeper re-reads the agent definition file every tick — read-the-file, fresh, inside the tick. There is no cache to invalidate. So editing the def — or a git pull replacing it — is live on the next tick… with nothing restarting. Deploying a new agent personality… is saving a file. [excited] And that gives us the boundary map — three rows. First — a toolkit command, the wasm: the swap lands on the next call, by registry repoint, in-flight safe. Second — an agent def or skill, the org file: it lands on the next tick, re-read per run, no cache. Third — content or blog: it lands on commit, where commit means publish, atomically. Three artifacts… three latencies… one idea. The live thing is a pointer, and the pointer is cheap to move. Nothing in that table involves a restart… because nothing in it is the engine.

tracks.title: The guardrails
tracks.text: A depth rung — skippable. The guardrails. Casual swapping is only safe because a handful of rules make the dangerous swaps impossible… rather than discouraged. Four carry the weight. First — built-ins are unshadowable. Trusted names like jq, grep, and upper are reserved, and the registry merges built-ins last at lookup. So even a poisoned key bound to jq loses. A swap can never replace a trusted built-in. Second — a hard cap, for a real reason. The dynamic registry tops out at four thousand ninety-six entries. Not arbitrary — every write to that table triggers a global garbage collection, so an unbounded registration storm is a denial-of-service. The cap makes the freedom un-weaponizable. Third — name hygiene. Names must match a strict character set… empty or exotic names refused at the door. And fourth — provenance gates the swap-in. A third-party toolkit with invalid provenance never builds — the engine refuses it, and tells the author to sign it first. Trust posture even drives the isolation tier… a third-party command runs in a separate BEAM VM, further from the core than your own. [curious] None of these slow the common case — your own signed tools, swapping in seconds. They exist so the freedom to swap can't be turned against the engine that grants it.

tracks.title: The same pattern elsewhere
tracks.text: Another depth rung. The same pattern… elsewhere. Once you see name… to content-addressed bytes… replace in place — you start seeing it everywhere. It's one idea reused, not three coincidences. The pallet — the prebuilt WASI artifacts — re-seeds idempotently… re-seeding replaces the binding in place. The kernel registry is the kernel-shaped twin of the command registry, in forty-five lines — same table, same four-thousand-ninety-six ceiling, same replace-in-place. Commands and kernels swap by the identical move. [excited] And the autopoet rides this as its whole job. It's the agent whose work is implementing capability issues filed by other agents — by editing the declarative config layer, never native code. Its edits land as org files, build through the same gates… and swap in live. The autopoet is what hot-swap looks like… as a standing practice… instead of a one-off.

tracks.title: Where it stops
tracks.text: The honest part — where it stops. And the most important limit is the most reassuring one. The host layer does not hot-swap. Engine code ships via the CI-built runtime image — that's a redeploy, not a swap. This isn't a gap… it's the design's spine. Loaded artifacts can be edited freely because the engine that loads them is fixed beneath them. Agent self-modification is safe… precisely because the agent can only ever touch the loaded layer… never the floor it stands on. The rest of the boundary, plainly — read the bottom rows together, because that's where a push won't just go live. App dist lands on pull. But app source needing vite lands only after CI, or a committed dist — that's the build seam, the project's own honestly-named gap. The host engine lands only on redeploy, never hot. And wbx itself lands on the next invocation, by a binary rename. [sighs] Two more honest notes. The reconcile trigger is a poll at each tick… not a webhook — a dedicated endpoint is the next step, not a shipped one. And the toolkit rebuild is a verb… not a daemon — a pull republishes content and deploys a committed dist, but it won't automatically rebuild a compiled command when source changes. For contrast — wbx upgrade swaps the CLI's own native binary, by downloading a new one and renaming it into place. Same word… different layer. The registry swap is live and in-flight-safe. The binary swap… waits for you to run the tool again.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Does an in-flight call see the new version? No. A call resolves its file at call time and keeps it to the end. Old bytes are never deleted, so anything running finishes on what it started with. Can a swap replace jq or grep? No — built-ins are reserved, and merged last at lookup. Trying it returns error, reserved name. What survives a reboot? The content store, plus a tiny manifest of name to path — on boot the engine re-registers every entry, no rebuild. Can someone swap a tampered artifact in? The filename is the sha of the trusted bytes, re-hashed at run time and refused on mismatch — so a byte altered after registration fails closed. Why didn't my pushed Svelte change go live? The build seam — a pull can't run vite on the BEAM box. Commit the built dist, or let CI build it. And — is this just Erlang hot code loading? [chuckles] Same spirit, different layer. Erlang swaps modules inside the VM. The Nexus swaps the artifacts the engine loads — and the engine's own code, notably, does not hot-swap.

tracks.title: Back up to the parent
tracks.text: So that's hot swap. A loaded artifact, replaced by repointing a name at new immutable bytes — in-flight work safe, nothing rebooting, and the host engine deliberately left out, because that fixed floor is what makes self-edits safe. [curious] Three vehicles got you here — the agent re-registering a tool it built, the git push reconciled at the next tick, and the def that swaps just by being re-read. If any of it felt unfamiliar… the way back up is short. This is a sub-lesson under nexus — lesson two — the engine you own. Start there… and everything the swap touches… is just the layer that engine loads.
